passage:
Monday: After the lie about the sleepover, Papa took Sunaina's phone, cancelled her dance class and said she would come straight home from school for two months. Her father, Vikas, had never been so angry. "No more chances," he said.
The next Thursday: Sunaina borrowed a friend's old phone and hid it inside a sock in her cupboard. She messaged only after midnight, with the screen brightness at zero.
Three weeks later: Papa asked, "You've been good lately, na?" Sunaina said, "Yes, Papa." She had become excellent at hiding, and not at all better at telling him things. Neither of them knew why the other felt so far away.

qa.q: Where did Sunaina hide the borrowed phone?
qa.a: She hid it inside a sock in her cupboard.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's "Yes, Papa" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels she must keep up an act; she has become good at hiding rather than trusting her father.

qa.q: What could Vikas have done instead of only restrictions?
qa.a: He could have set firm but fair limits and asked why Sunaina lied, so they could reset rules she could keep honestly.

qa.q: What is Vikas experiencing three weeks later?
qa.a: Vikas thinks things are better, but he feels a distance he can't explain, not knowing about the hidden phone.

grounding: Shows a teen girl who, after heavy punishment for a lie, learns to hide her phone use better instead of telling her father more.

passage: Ankita, sit. You're angry with your mother about the phone rule, I know. Let me tell you something about her. When your mother was fifteen, she lied to me about a school trip and went to the beach with friends. I was furious. I locked away her radio, stopped her going out for three months, and read every letter that came to the house. I thought I was teaching her honesty. What I actually taught her was to post her letters from her friend's house and to smile at me at dinner. She told me years later, after you were born. I had wanted to know why she lied. I never asked. Your grandpa Francis was strict, but not very wise. Don't tell your mother I said so.

qa.q: What did Francis lock away?
qa.a: He locked away her radio.

qa.q: What did Francis think he was teaching his daughter?
qa.a: Furious at her lie, he thought he was teaching her honesty, but she learnt to hide things better instead.

qa.q: What does Francis wish he had done differently?
qa.a: He wishes he had asked why she lied instead of only punishing, since he never learnt the reason.

qa.q: How might Ankita's mother have felt during those three months?
qa.a: She probably felt watched and resentful, so she kept up smiles at dinner while quietly posting letters from her friend's house.

grounding: Shows, through a grandfather's memory, a teen daughter who met heavy punishment for a lie by hiding better rather than telling more.

passage:
Uma,

I'm writing this in the school library because at home, they check everything now.
After they found out about the café, Papa took my phone for a month. No going out, no friends over, not even the tuition group chat. Mummy reads my notebooks. Their only daughter, under house arrest.
So you know what I've done? I've borrowed my cousin's old phone. I keep it in my pencil box and switch it off before I get home. I delete everything.
I'm not proud. But I'm not going to tell them anything now. Why would I? They didn't even ask why I lied. They just locked everything.
Write back by hand.

Neelam

qa.q: Where does Neelam keep her cousin's old phone?
qa.a: In her pencil box.

qa.q: What is Neelam feeling about her parents' restrictions?
qa.a: She feels resentful and shut out, and determined to hide more instead of telling them anything.

qa.q: What turning point could change this stage?
qa.a: Her parents could ask why she lied and talk about fairer terms, rather than relying only on heavy restrictions that push her to hide.

qa.q: What might Neelam's parents be experiencing?
qa.a: They are likely hurt and scared after the lie, and may believe the strict rules are keeping her safe, not knowing they are teaching her to hide.

grounding: A teenage girl under heavy restrictions after a lie starts hiding her phone use better instead of telling more, because nobody asked why she lied.

passage:
You want to know what happened after they found out? I'm Yamini, and I'll tell you exactly.
My mother took my phone, my laptop, and my allowance. No friends. No weekend outings. For two months.
I'd always been the good girl. And did I learn my lesson? Sort of. I learned how to hide better. I used Rajni's phone at school. I told my mother I was at the library and met my friends in the park behind it instead. I became really good at deleting chats.
Nobody at home ever asked why I lied in the first place. They just punished. So I figured, if honesty gets you punished and lying gets you punished too, why not just be better at lying?
I'm not saying it was right. I'm saying that's what happened.

qa.q: Whose phone did Yamini use at school?
qa.a: Rajni's phone.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling during the months of punishment?
qa.a: She felt resentful and unheard, deciding that honesty wasn't worth it because nobody asked why she lied.

qa.q: What turning point was missed at this stage?
qa.a: Her mother could have asked why Yamini lied and set clearer, fairer terms, rather than heavy punishment that taught hiding.

qa.q: What might Yamini's mother have been experiencing during those months?
qa.a: She likely felt betrayed and worried, and may have thought the strict rules were working without knowing Yamini was hiding more.

grounding: A teen describes how heavy punishment after a lie taught her to hide better rather than tell more, because nobody asked why she lied.

passage:
Monday: Papa found out Gargi had lied about the school trip. He took her phone and said no outings for six weeks. Jatin, her older brother, watched from the sofa.
Wednesday: Gargi started using the school computer lab to message her friends at lunch. She cleared the history every time. At dinner she said, "School was fine," and nothing else.
Saturday: Jatin found her whispering on the landline in the corridor. "Don't tell Papa," she said. Her voice was flat, not guilty any more, just careful. She had stopped telling anyone anything.

qa.q: How long were Gargi's outings banned?
qa.a: For six weeks.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling by Saturday?
qa.a: She seemed guarded and resentful, careful rather than guilty, having stopped telling anyone anything.

qa.q: What turning point could still help Gargi and her father?
qa.a: Papa could sit down with Gargi to learn why she lied about the trip and agree fairer terms, instead of relying only on the ban.

qa.q: What is Jatin experiencing as he watches?
qa.a: He likely feels uneasy and torn, seeing his sister hide more and being asked to keep her secret.

grounding: Over a week, heavy restrictions after a lie teach a teenage girl to hide her communication better rather than tell her father more.

passage:
Nandini, you think your Aparna Mausi was always so sensible? Listen.

When I was sixteen, I lied to your Nana about a cinema trip. He found out. That night he took my phone, my cycle key and cancelled my music class. No going out for three months.

Did I become honest? No, beta. I became clever. I borrowed my friend's old phone and kept it in my geometry box. I learned to delete every message. I told him less, not more.

He thought the punishment was working because the house was quiet. It wasn't working. I was just hiding better.

Years later I told him, and he looked so sad. He said, "I only wanted to know why you didn't ask me." But he never asked me that then. That was the missed turn. So when you mess up, I'll ask you why first.

qa.q: Where did Aparna hide the borrowed phone?
qa.a: She kept it in her geometry box.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling during those three months of punishment?
qa.a: She felt resentful and defensive, so she focused on hiding better rather than being more honest.

qa.q: What was the missed turning point inside the story?
qa.a: Nana could have asked why she hadn't asked him about the cinema and reset the rules, instead of only punishing.

qa.q: How did Aparna's father feel when he learned the truth years later?
qa.a: He felt sad, realising that his heavy punishment had taught hiding when he had only wanted to understand.

grounding: An elder recalls how strict punishment after a lie taught her to hide better rather than be honest, when the reason needed hearing.
